claim: During the development of the Drosophila brain, a travelling wave of proneural gene expression initiates neurogenesis in the larval optic lobe primordium.
source: During the development of the largest component of the visual processing centre of the Drosophila brain, a travelling wave of proneural gene expression initiates neurogenesis in the larval optic lobe primordium and drives the sequential transition of neuroepithelial cells into neuroblasts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known developmental process in Drosophila.

claim: The proneural wave drives the sequential transition of neuroepithelial cells into neuroblasts.
source: During the development of the largest component of the visual processing centre of the Drosophila brain, a travelling wave of proneural gene expression initiates neurogenesis in the larval optic lobe primordium and drives the sequential transition of neuroepithelial cells into neuroblasts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known developmental process.

claim: The proneural wave is driven by an excitable reaction-diffusion system involving EGFR signalling interacting with the proneural gene l'sc.
source: Here, we propose that this 'proneural wave' is driven by an excitable reaction-diffusion system involving epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signalling interacting with the proneural gene l'sc.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their modeling and experimental work.

claim: A propagating transition zone emerges from molecular feedback and diffusion within the proneural wave framework.
source: Within this framework, a propagating transition zone emerges from molecular feedback and diffusion.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ectopic activation of EGFR signalling in clones within the neuroepithelium demonstrates that a transition wave can be excited anywhere in the tissue.
source: Ectopic activation of EGFR signalling in clones within the neuroepithelium demonstrates that a transition wave can be excited anywhere in the tissue by inducing signalling activity, consistent with a key prediction of the model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Travelling waves are a ubiquitous feature of developmental pattern formation.
source: Such travelling waves, which are viable carriers of spatiotemporal information, are a ubiquitous feature of developmental pattern formation, where they arise through different underlying mechanisms, from coordinated intracellular oscillations (Oates et al., 2012; Jörg et al., 2015; Hubaud et al., 2017; Verd et al., 2018) to self-organised reaction-diffusion processes (Lubensky et al., 2011; Formosa-Jordan et al., 2012; Fried et al., 2016; Gavish et al., 2016; Corson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Neuroepithelial cells in the optic lobe divide symmetrically, expanding the progenitor pool.
source: neuroepithelial cells in the optic lobe of the larval brain divide symmetrically, expanding the progenitor pool, and then undergo a sequential transition into asymmetrically dividing neuroblasts, which generate the neurons of the medulla (Figure 1a,b) (Egger et al., 2007; Yasugi et al., 2008; Egger et al., 2010; Yasugi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations and Figure 1.

claim: Neuroepithelial cells undergo a sequential transition into asymmetrically dividing neuroblasts, which generate the neurons of the medulla.
source: neuroepithelial cells in the optic lobe of the larval brain divide symmetrically, expanding the progenitor pool, and then undergo a sequential transition into asymmetrically dividing neuroblasts, which generate the neurons of the medulla (Figure 1a,b) (Egger et al., 2007; Yasugi et al., 2008; Egger et al., 2010; Yasugi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations and Figure 1.

claim: The transition from neuroepithelial cells to neuroblasts occurs at a 'transition zone' that sweeps from one side of the optic lobe to the other.
source: The transition from neuroepithelial cells to neuroblasts occurs at a 'transition zone' that sweeps from one side of the optic lobe to the other and is marked by the expression of the proneural gene lethal of scute (l'sc) (Yasugi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The transition zone is marked by the expression of the proneural gene lethal of scute (l'sc).
source: The transition from neuroepithelial cells to neuroblasts occurs at a 'transition zone' that sweeps from one side of the optic lobe to the other and is marked by the expression of the proneural gene lethal of scute (l'sc) (Yasugi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The proneural wave is controlled by the coordinated action of EGFR signalling and Delta-Notch signalling.
source: This 'proneural wave' is controlled by the coordinated action of different signalling pathways: epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signalling and Delta-Notch signalling (Figure 1c–f) (Yasugi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation and Figure 1.

claim: The sequential nature of the transition is crucial to generate populations of cells of different developmental ages that give rise to a diverse array of terminally differentiated medulla neurons.
source: The sequential nature of the transition is crucial to generate populations of cells of different developmental ages that give rise to a diverse array of terminally differentiated medulla neurons (Li et al., 2013; Sato et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013; Erclik et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The transition zone exhibits localised EGFR signalling as well as expression of l'sc.
source: The transition zone exhibits localised EGFR signalling as well as expression of l'sc (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by Figure 1.

claim: Absence of EGFR signalling leads to loss of the differentiation wave.
source: Absence of EGFR signalling leads to loss of the differentiation wave, indicating that EGFR signalling is a key component for proneural wave progression (Yasugi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: EGFR signalling is a key component for proneural wave progression.
source: Absence of EGFR signalling leads to loss of the differentiation wave, indicating that EGFR signalling is a key component for proneural wave progression (Yasugi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The neuroepithelium exhibits low levels of Notch signalling activity.
source: The neuroepithelium exhibits low levels of Notch signalling activity (Egger et al., 2011; Weng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Notch activity peaks directly before the transition from neuroepithelial cell to neuroblast, drops during the transition and then is restored upon neuroblast transformation.
source: However, Notch activity peaks directly before the transition from neuroepithelial cell to neuroblast, drops during the transition and then is restored upon neuroblast transformation (Figure 1c) (Contreras et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation and Figure 1.

claim: The JAK/STAT and Fat-Hippo pathways play coordinating roles and prevent premature and ectopic transition of the neuroepithelium.
source: In addition, coordinating roles are played by the JAK/STAT and Fat-Hippo pathways, which are broadly expressed in the neuroepithelium and prevent premature and ectopic transition of the neuroepithelium (Yasugi et al., 2008; Yasugi et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2011a; Reddy et al., 2010; Kawamori et al., 2011; Weng et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: EGFR signalling activates the expression of L'sc.
source: EGFR signalling activates the expression of L'sc (Yasugi et al., 2010), which is sufficient to drive the neuroepithelium to neuroblast (NE to NB) transition (Yasugi et al., 2008; Contreras et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: L'sc expression is sufficient to drive the neuroepithelium to neuroblast (NE to NB) transition.
source: EGFR signalling activates the expression of L'sc (Yasugi et al., 2010), which is sufficient to drive the neuroepithelium to neuroblast (NE to NB) transition (Yasugi et al., 2008; Contreras et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The EGFR is activated by binding the secreted form of its ligand, Spitz.
source: The EGFR is activated by binding the secreted form of its ligand, Spitz.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge.

claim: Secreted Spitz is generated by cleavage of a membrane-bound precursor by the transmembrane protease, Rhomboid.
source: Secreted Spitz is generated by cleavage of a membrane-bound precursor by the transmembrane protease, Rhomboid (Klämbt, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: EGFR, Rhomboid and secreted Spitz together form an autocrine positive feedback loop.
source: EGFR, Rhomboid and secreted Spitz together form an autocrine positive feedback loop (Figure 1d) (Wiley et al., 2003; Sato et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations and Figure 1.

claim: The dynamics of EGFR signalling alone has features that are sufficient to enable sequential induction and produce a travelling front of EGFR signalling activity.
source: In a first step, we noted that the dynamics of EGFR signalling alone has features that are sufficient to enable such a sequential induction and produce a travelling front of EGFR signalling activity; a feature notably absent in recent attempts to model the proneural wave, which also require further components to stabilise the propagating EGFR signalling front (Sato et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reaction-diffusion systems involving diffusion and self-activation are known to support travelling bistable fronts that leave behind an elevated signalling state.
source: Generically, reaction-diffusion systems involving diffusion and self-activation are known to support travelling bistable fronts that leave behind an elevated signalling state (Figure 2a; Video 1; Appendix 1) (Muratov and Shvartsman, 2004; Keener and Sneyd, 2009; Graham et al., 2010; Tayar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations and Figure 2a.

claim: EGFR signalling is both necessary and sufficient for wave progression.
source: EGFR signalling is a natural candidate for being a key driver of the proneural wave and experimental evidence has shown that EGFR signalling is both necessary and sufficient for wave progression (Yasugi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The EGFR/Rhomboid/Spitz feedback loop does not remain active in the wake of the travelling wave, but remains spatially confined as Rhomboid is expressed only transiently in the travelling transition zone.
source: However, notably, the EGFR/Rhomboid/Spitz feedback loop does not remain active in the wake of the travelling wave, but remains spatially confined as Rhomboid is expressed only transiently in the travelling transition zone (Yasugi et al., 2010; Sato et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Elevated EGFR signalling activates L'sc expression.
source: Elevated EGFR signalling activates L'sc expression (Yasugi et al., 2010), which is sufficient to drive the NE to NB transition (Yasugi et al., 2008; Contreras et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: L'sc downregulates EGFR signalling as a consequence of the NE to NB transition, leading to an indirect negative feedback.
source: In this minimal model, L'sc downregulates EGFR signalling as a consequence of the transition, leading to an indirect negative feedback (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a feature of the model presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The reaction-diffusion system for EGFR signalling and L'sc expression can give rise to a travelling localised pulse of signalling activity and L'sc expression through the tissue.
source: Simulations of Equation 2 demonstrate that this type of feedback is sufficient to describe a travelling localised pulse of signalling activity and L'sc expression through the tissue (Figure 2b,c; Video 2; Appendix 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulations shown in Figure 2b,c and Video 2.

claim: The dynamics of L'sc alter the bistable signalling behaviour of EGFR signalling into an excitable one.
source: Notably, the dynamics of L'sc (L) alter the bistable signalling behaviour of EGFR signalling (E) into an excitable one: once sufficiently perturbed by diffusion from an adjacent cell with an elevated signalling state, the intracellular reaction dynamics produces a transient expression pulse that downregulates itself as a result of the NE to NB cell fate transition (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Delta-Notch signalling influences how long cells remain in the L'sc expressing state.
source: We next aimed to develop a more refined model that could be challenged by experiment and compared with previously published data. Such a model necessarily includes Delta-Notch signalling, which has been shown to influence how long cells remain in the L'sc expressing state (Yasugi et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2011b; Weng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Delta-Notch signalling is often associated with the emergence of 'salt-and-pepper'-like patterns of cell fate.
source: As a mediator of lateral inhibition, Delta-Notch signalling is often associated with the emergence of 'salt-and-pepper'-like patterns of cell fate (Bray, 2006; Shaya and Sprinzak, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The 'salt-and-pepper' pattern is not seen during proneural wave progression.
source: However, this pattern is not seen during proneural wave progression and the reasons for this are not clear (Egger et al., 2010; Pérez-Gómez et al., 2013; Sato et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The integrated model includes canonical Delta-Notch interactions: trans-activation of Notch by Delta, downregulation of Delta by Notch within the same cell, and cis-inhibition.
source: To address this question, we extended our minimal model to include canonical Delta-Notch interactions (Figure 2d) (Collier et al., 1996; Bray, 2006; Simakov and Pismen, 2013): (i) trans-activation of Notch by Delta, (ii) downregulation of Delta by Notch within the same cell and (iii) cis-inhibition (downregulation of Notch by Delta in the same cell).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations and Figure 2d.

claim: The model incorporates upregulation of Delta through EGFR signalling.
source: The model incorporates interactions between the Delta-Notch signalling pathway, EGFR signalling and L'sc expression, namely, upregulation of Delta through EGFR signalling (Yasugi et al., 2010), upregulation of EGFR signalling through Notch signalling (Yasugi et al., 2010), downregulation of L'sc through Notch signalling (Reddy et al., 2010) and downregulation of Notch expression through L'sc (Egger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The model incorporates upregulation of EGFR signalling through Notch signalling.
source: The model incorporates interactions between the Delta-Notch signalling pathway, EGFR signalling and L'sc expression, namely, upregulation of Delta through EGFR signalling (Yasugi et al., 2010), upregulation of EGFR signalling through Notch signalling (Yasugi et al., 2010), downregulation of L'sc through Notch signalling (Reddy et al., 2010) and downregulation of Notch expression through L'sc (Egger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The model incorporates downregulation of L'sc through Notch signalling.
source: The model incorporates interactions between the Delta-Notch signalling pathway, EGFR signalling and L'sc expression, namely, upregulation of Delta through EGFR signalling (Yasugi et al., 2010), upregulation of EGFR signalling through Notch signalling (Yasugi et al., 2010), downregulation of L'sc through Notch signalling (Reddy et al., 2010) and downregulation of Notch expression through L'sc (Egger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The model incorporates downregulation of Notch expression through L'sc.
source: The model incorporates interactions between the Delta-Notch signalling pathway, EGFR signalling and L'sc expression, namely, upregulation of Delta through EGFR signalling (Yasugi et al., 2010), upregulation of EGFR signalling through Notch signalling (Yasugi et al., 2010), downregulation of L'sc through Notch signalling (Reddy et al., 2010) and downregulation of Notch expression through L'sc (Egger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The functional 'module' comprising EGFR signalling and L'sc expression remains the driver of the wave.
source: Despite these complex interactions, the functional 'module' comprising EGFR signalling and L'sc expression still remains the driver of the wave (green box in Figure 2d), while Delta-Notch signalling acts to provide further timing cues for the transition and to prevent premature differentiation (pink box in Figure 2d) (Egger et al., 2010; Reddy et al., 2010; Yasugi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations and Figure 2d.

claim: Delta-Notch signalling acts to provide further timing cues for the transition and to prevent premature differentiation.
source: Despite these complex interactions, the functional 'module' comprising EGFR signalling and L'sc expression still remains the driver of the wave (green box in Figure 2d), while Delta-Notch signalling acts to provide further timing cues for the transition and to prevent premature differentiation (pink box in Figure 2d) (Egger et al., 2010; Reddy et al., 2010; Yasugi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations and Figure 2d.

claim: The NE to NB transition is promoted by L'sc.
source: The NE to NB transition is promoted by L'sc (Yasugi et al., 2008) and downregulation of Notch in the presence of EGFR signalling (Yasugi et al., 2010; Weng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The NE to NB transition is promoted by downregulation of Notch in the presence of EGFR signalling.
source: The NE to NB transition is promoted by L'sc (Yasugi et al., 2008) and downregulation of Notch in the presence of EGFR signalling (Yasugi et al., 2010; Weng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The integrated model yielded predictions on the spatial profiles of signalling activity and gene expression that were in striking agreement with features observed in prior experiments.
source: In addition to the emergence of a propagating transition zone, the integrated model also yielded predictions on the spatial profiles of signalling activity and gene expression (Figure 2e; Figure 4a; Video 3; Video 4; Appendix 4), which were in striking agreement with features observed in prior experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figures 2e and 4a.

claim: EGFR signalling, as well as L'sc and Delta expression, is elevated only in the transition zone.
source: First, EGFR signalling, as well as L'sc and Delta expression, was found to be elevated only in the transition zone (Figure 1c) (Egger et al., 2010; Yasugi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations and Figure 1c.

claim: A peak of Notch activity is observed slightly in advance of the transition zone followed by a sharp drop in Notch activity.
source: Second, a peak of Notch activity is observed slightly in advance of the transition zone (pink arrowheads in Figure 2e) followed by a sharp drop in Notch activity (Figure 1c) (Egger et al., 2011; Orihara-Ono et al., 2011; Weng et al., 2012; Contreras et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations and Figures 1c and 2e.

claim: According to the model, lateral inhibition promotes high-Delta/low-Notch and low-Delta/high-Notch states in adjacent cells, and leads to a travelling 'laterally inhibited' cell state as the wave progresses.
source: According to the model, lateral inhibition promotes high-Delta/low-Notch and low-Delta/high-Notch states in adjacent cells, and leads to a travelling 'laterally inhibited' cell state as the wave progresses.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The drop in Notch levels in transitioning cells arises due to cis-inhibition as a consequence of Delta binding to Notch within the same cell.
source: By contrast, the drop in Notch levels in transitioning cells arises due to cis-inhibition in our model as a consequence of Delta binding to Notch within the same cell, as has been shown experimentally (Reddy et al., 2010; Weng et al., 2012; Contreras et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a prediction of the model that is supported by experimental citations.

claim: The model captured the acceleration, delay or loss of the proneural wavefront within a clone depending upon its genetic makeup.
source: Consistent with experiment, the model captured the acceleration, delay or loss of the proneural wavefront within a clone depending upon its genetic makeup (Figure 3a–f; Appendix 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3.

claim: Clones in which EGFR signalling has been constitutively activated tend to advance the transition zone within the clone.
source: For example, clones in which EGFR signalling has been constitutively activated tend to advance the transition zone within the clone, while the absence of EGFR signalling leads to loss of the proneural wave (Figure 3a,b) (Yasugi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation and Figure 3.

claim: The absence of EGFR signalling leads to loss of the proneural wave.
source: For example, clones in which EGFR signalling has been constitutively activated tend to advance the transition zone within the clone, while the absence of EGFR signalling leads to loss of the proneural wave (Figure 3a,b) (Yasugi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation and Figure 3.

claim: Low levels of Notch signalling activity are observed both in the neuroepithelium and in neuroblasts but not at the transition zone.
source: Low levels of Notch signalling activity are observed both in the neuroepithelium and in neuroblasts but not at the transition zone (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1c.

claim: Notch activity is required to maintain neuroepithelial cell fate and the loss of Notch results in premature transformation into neuroblasts.
source: It has been shown experimentally that Notch activity is required to maintain neuroepithelial cell fate and the loss of Notch results in premature transformation into neuroblasts (Egger et al., 2010; Ngo et al., 2010; Reddy et al., 2010; Yasugi et al., 2010; Orihara-Ono et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011b; Pérez-Gómez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Despite the observation of active Notch signalling, there is no evidence of lateral inhibition in the neuroepithelium.
source: Intriguingly, despite the observation of active Notch signalling, there is no evidence of lateral inhibition in the neuroepithelium.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation.

claim: The model predicts that the basal level of Notch activity observed in the neuroepithelium could be the reason for the suppression of lateral inhibition patterns outside the transition zone.
source: Notably, our model predicts that the basal level of Notch activity observed in the the neuroepithelium could be the reason for the suppression of lateral inhibition patterns outside the transition zone.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the model, basal levels of Notch activity in the neuroepithelium lead to a spatially homogeneous 'oversaturation' that prevents the Delta levels from rising before being activated by EGFR signalling.
source: In our model, basal levels of Notch activity in the neuroepithelium lead to a spatially homogeneous 'oversaturation' that prevents the Delta levels from rising before being activated by EGFR signalling.
evidence: This is a feature of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: If basal Notch levels are lowered to small values compared to the threshold levels for activation and inhibition in the model, salt-and-pepper patterns that are a consequence of lateral inhibition are recapitulated.
source: However, if basal Notch levels are lowered to small values compared to the threshold levels for activation and inhibition in our model, we indeed recapitulate the salt-and-pepper patterns that are a consequence of lateral inhibition (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a prediction of the model shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Downregulation of Notch levels by expressing Notch RNAi in clones does not result in the emergence of a salt-and-pepper expression pattern of Delta.
source: We tested this prediction of the model by lowering Notch levels in the neuroepithelium but we did not observe 'salt-and-pepper' patterns of Delta/Notch expression within clones expressing an RNAi against Notch (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The absence of the emergence of lateral inhibition is likely due to the complete loss of detectable Notch in cells expressing the RNAi.
source: However, the absence of the emergence of lateral inhibition is likely due to the complete loss of detectable Notch in cells expressing the RNAi (Figure 4d), while the reduction of Notch levels in the model prediction is more subtle (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental result shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Both basal and Delta-regulated Notch activity need to be in the appropriate range for lateral inhibition patterns to occur.
source: Referring to the 'phase diagram' in Figure 4e, it can be seen that both basal and Delta-regulated Notch activity need to be in the appropriate range for lateral inhibition patterns to occur, which is difficult to achieve experimentally.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The model entails that Notch downregulation is a necessary (but not generally sufficient) condition for inducing salt-and-pepper patterns.
source: Furthermore, our model entails that Notch downregulation is a necessary (but not generally sufficient) condition for inducing salt-and-pepper patterns.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model.

claim: The diffusion, gain and decay rate of EGFR signalling are the key regulators of wave speed.
source: As expected, this analysis showed that the diffusion, gain and decay rate of EGFR signalling (η, μE and kE) are the key regulators of wave speed, since EGFR signalling constitutes the driver of the wave in our model (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a result of the sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: L'sc gene expression had almost no effect on wave speed since its dynamics is 'pulled' by the EGFR signalling front.
source: In contrast, L'sc gene expression (parametrised by μL and kL) had almost no effect on wave speed since its dynamics is 'pulled' by the EGFR signalling front.
evidence: This is a result of the sensitivity analysis.

claim: The basal gain rate of Notch signalling as well as its decay rate play another prominent role in setting the wave speed.
source: Interestingly, the basal gain rate of Notch signalling (β) as well as its decay rate (kN) play another prominent role in setting the wave speed.
evidence: This is a result of the sensitivity analysis.

claim: Notch signalling promotes EGFR signalling at the transition zone, leading to a reinforcement of activation as the wave arrives at undifferentiated cells.
source: This is consistent with experimental data showing that Notch signalling promotes EGFR signalling at the transition zone, leading to a reinforcement of activation as the wave arrives at undifferentiated cells (Yasugi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: L'sc expression had a tightening effect on the width of the transition zone as it promoted differentiation and therefore leads to a faster termination of differentiation.
source: Considering the width of the transition zone (Figure 5b), we found that while all parameters had some effect, L'sc expression clearly had a tightening effect as it promoted differentiation and therefore leads to a faster termination of differentiation.
evidence: This is a result of the sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Basal Notch signalling in the epithelium tended to enlarge the width of the transition zone in the sensitivity analysis.
source: In contrast, basal Notch signalling in the epithelium (described by β and kN) tended to enlarge the width of the transition zone in our sensitivity analysis.
evidence: This is a result of the sensitivity analysis.

claim: Overexpression of Notch at the transition zone extends the width of the L'sc stripe and delays the transformation into neuroblasts.
source: Indeed, a recent study showed that overexpression of Notch at the transition zone extends the width of the L'sc stripe and delays the transformation into neuroblasts (Contreras et al., 2018), providing support for this prediction of the model.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: A complementary prediction of the model is that a reduction of Notch at the transition zone would decrease the width of the L'sc stripe.
source: Subsequently, it follows that a complementary prediction of the model would be that a reduction of Notch at the transition zone would decrease the width of the L'sc stripe.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model.

claim: Within clones expressing Notch RNAi, the proneural wave was accelerated.
source: Within clones expressing Notch RNAi, the proneural wave was not only accelerated (Figure 3), as observed previously in Notch mutant clones (Egger et al., 2010; Reddy et al., 2010; Yasugi et al., 2010), but the width of the transition zone also appeared smaller (yellow arrowheads in Figure 6).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figures 3 and 6, and supported by citations.

claim: Within clones expressing Notch RNAi, the width of the transition zone appeared smaller.
source: Within clones expressing Notch RNAi, the proneural wave was not only accelerated (Figure 3), as observed previously in Notch mutant clones (Egger et al., 2010; Reddy et al., 2010; Yasugi et al., 2010), but the width of the transition zone also appeared smaller (yellow arrowheads in Figure 6).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 6.

claim: EGFR and Notch signalling are the key regulators of wave speed and width of the transition zone while L'sc expression provides an additional acceleration of the transition of the wave.
source: In summary, this sensitivity analysis suggests that EGFR and Notch signalling are the key regulators of wave speed and width of the transition zone while L'sc expression provides an additional acceleration of the transition of the wave and therefore has a negative influence on the width of the transition zone.
evidence: This is a summary of the sensitivity analysis results.

claim: Through interactions between L'sc and EGFR signalling, the neuroepithelium functions as an excitable medium.
source: A signature feature of the model dynamics is that, through interactions between L'sc and EGFR signalling, the neuroepithelium functions as an excitable medium.
evidence: This is a key feature of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model predicts that local induction of EGFR signalling would initiate a circular (target-like) transition wave.
source: As such, the model predicts that local induction of EGFR signalling would initiate a circular (target-like) transition wave (Figure 7a; Video 5).
evidence: This is a prediction of the model shown in Figure 7a and Video 5.

claim: Clones expressing PntP1 showed upregulation of L'sc at clonal boundaries and expression of Dpn within the clone, suggesting the ectopic generation of neuroblasts within the epithelium.
source: We found upregulation of L'sc at clonal boundaries and expression of Dpn within the clone, suggesting the ectopic generation of neuroblasts within the epithelium, that is, a NE to NB transition (Figure 7b,c).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 7b,c.

claim: The experimental results agree with previous experiments showing the induction of neuroblasts within the neuroepithelium in response to ectopic EGFR signalling.
source: Our results agree with previous experiments showing the induction of neuroblasts within the neuroepithelium in response to ectopic EGFR signalling (Yasugi et al., 2010) and are in striking agreement with model simulations based on the same perturbation (Figure 7a; Video 5; Supplementary Text).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation and Figure 7a.

claim: The proneural wave involves the activation of an excitatory pulse of signalling activity and gene expression, giving rise to a tightly-regulated propagating transition zone.
source: Our findings suggest that the proneural wave involves the activation of an excitatory pulse of signalling activity and gene expression, giving rise to a tightly-regulated propagating transition zone.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: The reaction-diffusion system described is based on strictly local inhibition, in contrast with Turing-based activator-inhibitor mechanisms which typically comprise fast diffusible inhibitors.
source: In contrast with Turing-based activator-inhibitor mechanisms (Turing, 1952), which typically comprise fast diffusible inhibitors, the reaction-diffusion system described here is based on strictly local inhibition (Figure 2b,c).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation and Figure 2b,c.

claim: The role of sequential patterning by the proneural wave is to ensure the correct timing and composition of the neuroblast population.
source: The role of sequential patterning by the proneural wave is to ensure the correct timing and composition of the neuroblast population (Bertet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: A similar process of sequential patterning occurs during the progression of the morphogenetic furrow in the Drosophila eye.
source: A similar process of sequential patterning occurs during the progression of the morphogenetic furrow in the Drosophila eye (Roignant and Treisman, 2009; Lubensky et al., 2011; Formosa-Jordan et al., 2012; Wartlick et al., 2014; Fried et al., 2016; Gavish et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The JAK/STAT and Hippo pathways serve important roles in modulating proneural wave progression but are not actively involved in propagating the transition zone through a reaction-diffusion-like mechanism.
